title: Calculate EER for an R22 refrigeration cycle
skills_assessed: Refrigerant property lookup and state-point definition
COP and EER calculation with non-ideal compression
Comparison to an inverse Carnot reference cycle

role.title: HVAC / refrigeration engineer
role.company_context: Commercial and light-industrial refrigeration contractor. Engineers size and check vapor-compression systems for cold rooms and process chillers, document cycle performance (COP/EER), and compare real machines to an ideal Carnot benchmark for design reviews and client reports.
day_to_day: Build thermodynamic state-point tables for vapor-compression cycles from design temperatures and refrigerant data
Look up refrigerant properties from tables, software, or online tools and document the source
Calculate refrigerating effect, compressor work, COP, and EER including compression efficiency
Compare cycle performance to an inverse Carnot reference that accounts for heat-exchanger temperature differences
Write clear calculation notes a senior engineer can review without guessing assumptions
required_skills: Can define evaporator, compressor, condenser, and expansion states for a simple vapor-compression cycle
Comfortable reading R22 (or similar) thermodynamic properties from tables or property software
Can apply isentropic and actual compression work with a given compression efficiency
Understands COP, EER, and COP of an inverse Carnot refrigerator
nice_to_have_skills: Familiarity with CoolProp, REFPROP, or manufacturer property software
Experience with p-h diagrams and suction-line superheat conventions
Prior cold-room or commercial refrigeration design work
constraints: Assessment is a thermodynamics calculation work sample — not building production software or a containerized app
Candidates may use any tools they like for refrigerant properties and arithmetic
Do not require paid licensed software beyond what is freely available on the desktop or online
Starter files on the desktop are shared scenery (parameters and a blank calculation template), not a solved answer

problem_statement.title: Calculate EER and Carnot-relative efficiency for an R22 system
problem_statement.summary: You are checking the thermodynamic performance of a simple vapor-compression refrigeration system using R22. Design data are fixed below. Produce a clear calculation of the actual cycle COP and EER, then compare performance to an inverse Carnot cycle with a 10 K temperature difference at both the evaporator and the condenser. You are free to use any tools you like (spreadsheets, calculators, CoolProp/REFPROP, ASHRAE or manufacturer tables, online property tools, etc.) to obtain R22 properties — document which source you used.
outcomes: Build a state-point table covering at least evaporator outlet, compressor inlet, compressor discharge, condenser outlet, and expansion-valve inlet.
Calculate refrigerating effect, compressor work (using the given compression efficiency), COP, and EER of the actual cycle.
Calculate the COP of the inverse Carnot reference with ΔT = 10 K at both evaporator and condenser, and the efficiency of the actual cycle relative to that Carnot COP.
constraints: Use the fixed design data: Tev = −10 °C; suction superheat = 10 K; useful superheat = 0 K; Tcond = +30 °C; refrigerant R22; compression efficiency η_comp = 0.7.
Interpret useful superheat 0 K as saturated vapor leaving the evaporator at Tev; interpret suction superheat 10 K as compressor inlet 10 K above saturation at evaporator pressure.
For the Carnot reference, apply ΔT = 10 K on both sides: T_cold = Tev − 10 K and T_hot = Tcond + 10 K.
State your assumptions and the property data source. Prefer concrete numbers and a readable state table over slogans.
problem_statement.deliverables: A written calculation (document, notes, or spreadsheet) that a reviewer can follow: state-point table with enthalpies (and other properties as needed), energy balances for q_evap and w_comp, COP, EER, Carnot COP, and Carnot-relative efficiency η_Carnot = COP_actual / COP_Carnot. Optionally attach working files from property software — not required if the written calculation is complete and consistent.

rubric.name: Cycle state-point analysis
rubric.description: Correctly identifies saturated vapor at Tev = −10 °C (useful superheat 0 K), compressor inlet with 10 K suction superheat at evaporator pressure, saturated liquid at Tcond = +30 °C, and isenthalpic expansion (h4 = h3).

rubric.name: COP and EER calculation
rubric.description: Enthalpy-based refrigerating effect and compressor work are coherent; η_comp = 0.7 is applied as W = W_isentropic / 0.7 (not inverted); COP and EER are reported with a correct EER conversion (EER ≈ COP × 3.412).

rubric.name: Carnot reference cycle
rubric.description: Uses ΔT = 10 K at both evaporator and condenser for T_cold and T_hot; applies COP_Carnot = T_cold / (T_hot − T_cold) with absolute temperatures; computes η_Carnot = COP_actual / COP_Carnot consistently.

rubric.name: Assumptions and data sourcing
rubric.description: States the refrigerant property source and visible cycle assumptions (e.g. negligible pressure drops, saturated liquid leaving the condenser, isenthalpic throttling).

rubric.name: Clarity of deliverable
rubric.description: Readable state table and final numbers a reviewer can follow without guessing intermediate steps or units.

invariants: Keep the same skills_assessed and rubric structure/weights
Keep the same deliverable kinds and difficulty band (written thermodynamics calculation with COP/EER and Carnot comparison)
Do not change workspace files that are not listed under variation.files
Do not turn the challenge into software engineering, containerization, or a multi-refrigerant parametric study

constraints: This challenge uses a shared problem statement for every candidate
Do not paraphrase or rewrite outcomes, constraints, or deliverables per instance
